clue.text: Police capital described by Seán O'Faoláin?

definitions.text: Police capital described by Seán O'Faoláin?

parts.words: Police capital described by Seán O'Faoláin?
parts.note: police are coppers and capital is money, so this is money held in coppers: the title of O'Faoláin's 1937 story collection, 'A ... of Coppers'

explanation.surface: A question about how an Irish writer portrayed the funds or the headquarters of the police.
explanation.walkthrough: Seán O'Faoláin, an Irish writer, published the collection 'A Purse of Coppers'; coppers is slang for police and also small coins.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bag for money holds a person's cash, their capital in a homely sense.

clue.text: CIA topics codified in collage

indicators.note: codified suggests put into a new coded order, so the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: Intelligence agency subjects encrypted into a patchwork artwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasticcio is a medley assembled from many sources, much as a collage is.

clue.text: Ardent youth has computer-type memory, ex officio

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in a computer
EO is the abbreviation for ex officio, by virtue of office

explanation.surface: A passionate young man equipped with a computer's memory, holding a post by right of office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is just a link joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's young lover gives his name to any passionate young suitor.

clue.text: "Restore, restore — to life" (Pope)

parts.note: the blank is filled from Pope's Ode on St Cecilia's Day, where Orpheus begs the underworld to give back his dead wife

explanation.surface: A line quoted from Alexander Pope with one name left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Pope's ode Orpheus sings 'Restore, restore Eurydice to life'; the solver supplies the missing name.
explanation.definitionFit: The wife of Orpheus, lost to the underworld, is the person the singer pleads to have brought back.

clue.text: Foundling in strange passé epic ( 4)

indicators.note: strange signals the letters of the phrase are made odd, that is rearranged

explanation.surface: An abandoned child appearing in an odd, outdated heroic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The '( 4)' in the clue as held looks like a stray print mark.
explanation.definitionFit: In George Eliot's Silas Marner, the child Eppie is a foundling left at the weaver's cottage.

clue.text: He paid dearly for his brother's soup

definitions.text: He paid dearly for his brother's soup

parts.words: He paid dearly for his brother's soup
parts.note: Genesis tells of the elder twin who sold his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of red pottage

explanation.surface: A man who was overcharged for a bowl of his sibling's broth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the hungry elder son of Isaac traded his birthright for Jacob's stew.

clue.text: Clergyman, supported by drinks, depicting rural life

indicators.note: in a down clue supported by means the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: a pastor is a minister of a church
ales are drinks of beer

explanation.surface: A minister propped up by beers, with country life as the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastorales are musical or dramatic works portraying the countryside and shepherds.

clue.text: A season of Strindberg

parts.note: both a spring festival season and the title of a 1901 play by the Swedish dramatist

explanation.surface: A theatre's run of plays by the Swedish dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Strindberg wrote a play named after the spring festival; 'season' looks like a theatre programme but is the church season.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring feast of the Resurrection is a church season and also a Strindberg play title.

clue.text: Sandy companion of Hannay

parts.note: Sandy is the first name of the friend who joins John Buchan's hero Richard Hannay in Greenmantle

explanation.surface: A red-haired friend of a fictional adventurer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandy' looks like a description of hair colour; it is the character's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy Arbuthnot is Richard Hannay's ally in John Buchan's thrillers.

clue.text: The point of Herbert's oeuvre

parts.note: point read as a sharp weapon tip rather than the purpose of a writer's work

explanation.surface: A question about what a writer's body of work is really for.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-shafted weapon with a sharp head is literally all point.

clue.text: A mess in Ur? a real mess, for its inhabitants

indicators.note: a real mess says the preceding letters are thoroughly jumbled

explanation.surface: Ancient Ur was in chaos, and so were the people living there.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient people of Sumer lived in cities such as Ur in Mesopotamia.

clue.text: A squadron of ravens spoken of -not an unkindness?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'A squadron of ravens spoken of -not an unkindness? (5)' gives no parse for SABRE: 'spoken of' wants a homophone but none fits, and no source gives the setter's reading.
annotationWithheld.clue: A squadron of ravens spoken of -not an unkindness?

clue.text: Mark's wife not so young, they say

indicators.note: they say signals that a spoken phrase gives the answer by sound

parts.note: someone not so young ..., and with 'is' from the surface sense (she ...) this gives the spoken phrase

explanation.surface: Gossip that Mark's spouse is no spring chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: Said in a non-rhotic accent, 'is older' (what 'not so young' says of the wife) sounds like the name.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Tristan legend the Irish princess marries King Mark of Cornwall.

clue.text: Novelist from before Sterne

indicators.note: from signals the letters are taken out of a run of the following words

explanation.surface: A writer who came earlier than Laurence Sterne.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the run of letters across 'before Sterne'; Sterne looks like the clue's subject.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Forester wrote the Hornblower novels.

clue.text: Pope keeps a retro miscellany for musical historian

indicators.note: keeps means the pope's name holds the other letters within it

parts.note: Pius is the name taken by many popes

indicators.note: a miscellany is a jumble, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: A pontiff holding on to a collection of old-fashioned odds and ends for a music scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope' looks like the poet in this literary puzzle, but it is a pontiff's name; the anagram of 'a retro' signalled by 'miscellany' goes after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Praetorius wrote Syntagma Musicum, a major early account of music and instruments.

clue.text: A stanza with connections to the crown?

definitions.text: A stanza with connections to the crown?

parts.words: A stanza with connections to the crown?
parts.note: rhyme royal is a seven-line verse form, royal suggesting the crown; it is named after the poet of Troilus and Criseyde

explanation.surface: A verse form somehow linked to royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhyme royal, the seven-line stanza, is also called the Chaucerian stanza; 'royal' is the link to the crown.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer used the rhyme royal stanza in Troilus and Criseyde, so it bears his name.

clue.text: Arab child perhaps as groom for Scott

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters may be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A child from Arabia proposed as a husband by Walter Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Archibald is a Scottish man's name, the sort of bridegroom Scott's novels marry off.

clue.text: Dramatist in the main gentle

indicators.note: in signals the letters lie inside the following words

explanation.surface: A playwright who is, for the most part, a mild man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' looks like the sea; the answer runs across 'main gentle'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Inge was an American playwright, author of Picnic and Bus Stop.

clue.text: Style Anne adapted in melodramatic novel

indicators.note: adapted means altered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman's manner reworked for a sensational book.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Henry Wood's Victorian sensation novel East Lynne became a byword for melodrama.

clue.text: Book in which to get one's bearings

definitions.text: Book in which to get one's bearings

parts.words: Book in which to get one's bearings
parts.note: bearings read in the heraldic sense, the devices on coats of arms, not directions

explanation.surface: A guidebook for finding one's way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearings' suggests navigation; in heraldry bearings are the charges on a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll of coats of arms records heraldic devices, the bearings of families.

clue.text: Alternatives include many middle earth ogres

indicators.note: include means the first word's letters hold the other inside

parts.note: ors are alternatives, as in 'no ifs or buts'
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many

explanation.surface: Options covering numerous monstrous Tolkien creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien's goblin-like brutes of Middle-earth are fearsome monsters.

clue.text: Pompey supporter makes Cretan seem unreliable

indicators.note: unreliable suggests the letters cannot be trusted to stay put, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A follower of Pompey makes a man from Crete look untrustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' is a link; Cretans were proverbial liars, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Menecrates is one of Pompey's pirate allies in Antony and Cleopatra.

clue.text: Ancient Shakespearean sidearm

definitions.meaning: an ancient is an ensign, the rank of Falstaff's swaggering follower in Henry V
a handgun carried at the side

explanation.definitionFit: Pistol is Falstaff's ensign in Shakespeare, and a pistol is a handgun.

clue.text: An operatic Tom Jones not one of his better gambits

definitions.text: An operatic Tom Jones not one of his better gambits

parts.words: An operatic Tom Jones not one of his better gambits
parts.note: a French composer of an opera on Fielding's novel was also the leading chess master of his day, with an opening named after him

explanation.surface: A singer's operatic outing judged a poor career move.
explanation.walkthrough: François-André Philidor wrote the opera Tom Jones and was a great chess player; 'Tom Jones' suggests the Welsh singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Philidor composed the opéra comique Tom Jones and gave his name to a chess defence.

clue.text: Prelude right in ode, perhaps

indicators.note: in means the letter is placed inside the other word

parts.note: an ode is an example of a poem

explanation.surface: An introduction placed properly in a lyric.
explanation.definitionFit: A proem is an introductory passage or preface.

clue.text: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing

definitions.text: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing

parts.words: He was early preoccupied with a question of upbringing
parts.note: A Question of Upbringing is the first, early volume of a twelve-novel sequence by Anthony of that surname

explanation.surface: A man who was concerned from youth about how children are raised.
explanation.walkthrough: A Question of Upbringing opens A Dance to the Music of Time; 'early' points to the first novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell wrote A Question of Upbringing as the first book of his sequence.

clue.text: Poet with features of clerical cut, not nice to meet

definitions.text: Poet with features of clerical cut, not nice to meet

parts.words: Poet with features of clerical cut, not nice to meet
parts.note: quotes a poet's self-mocking verse: 'How unpleasant to meet Mr ...! / With his features of clerical cut'

explanation.surface: A disagreeable poet with a priestly look.
explanation.walkthrough: T. S. Eliot's 'Lines for Cuscuscaraway and Mirza Murad Ali Beg' describes himself this way.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot mocked his own priestly face in light verse.

clue.text: Hellish flower, reportedly bonebreaker

indicators.note: reportedly signals the word as spoken

parts.note: 'sticks and stones may break my bones', so sticks break bones

explanation.surface: An infernal bloom that is said to snap bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is something that flows, a river, not a bloom; the Styx is the river of the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: The Styx is the river of Hades in Greek myth.

clue.text: Abstract style originates only partly as realist tendency (3)

indicators.note: originates points to where each word starts, its first letter

explanation.surface: A non-figurative manner of painting that grows partly out of a realist trend.
explanation.walkthrough: The '(3)' in the clue as held looks like a stray print mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is abstract art built on optical illusions.

clue.text: Instinctive knowledge from fashionable teaching

parts.note: in means fashionable
tuition is teaching

explanation.surface: Gut feeling acquired from trendy lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Intuition is understanding reached without reasoning, an instinctive grasp.

clue.text: Its rural parts our lost Elysium, thought Betjeman

definitions.text: Its rural parts our lost Elysium, thought Betjeman

parts.words: Its rural parts our lost Elysium, thought Betjeman
parts.note: Betjeman mourned the vanished countryside of the county north-west of London swallowed by suburbs

explanation.surface: John Betjeman lamenting the paradise lost in a place's countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Betjeman's poems, such as 'Middlesex', mourn the former English county north-west of London, now absorbed into Greater London.
explanation.definitionFit: Betjeman wrote nostalgically of the green fields of this former home county before suburban sprawl.

clue.text: "Whom, on the wharf of — waiting, / Count you to find?" (Housman)

definitions.text: "Whom, on the wharf of — waiting, / Count you to find?" (Housman)

parts.words: "Whom, on the wharf of — waiting, / Count you to find?" (Housman)
parts.note: the blank is the river of forgetfulness in Hades, where Housman pictures the dead waiting

explanation.surface: Lines from A. E. Housman with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: From Housman's 'Parta Quies'-era verse in More Poems; the wharf is on the underworld's river of oblivion.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the dead drink from the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.
